title: RAG or fine-tuning: how to choose for company knowledge
metaTitle: RAG vs Fine-Tuning for Company Knowledge: How to Choose
description: When to use retrieval-augmented generation, when to fine-tune a model, and when to combine them, explained for teams building AI on their own documents and data.
author: Mahsam Abbas
answer: Use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) when the AI must answer from your own documents and data, especially when that information changes or access to it is restricted. Use fine-tuning when you need the model to follow a consistent style, format or narrow task that prompting cannot achieve. For company knowledge, RAG is almost always the starting point, and fine-tuning is an optional later step.

sections.heading: What each one does
sections.text: RAG leaves the model unchanged. When a question arrives, the system searches your documents, passes the most relevant passages to the model, and asks it to answer from them with citations. Fine-tuning changes the model itself by training it further on examples, so the behaviour is built in.

sections.heading: Why RAG fits company knowledge
sections.text: Company knowledge has three properties that favour retrieval.
bullets: It changes. A new policy or price takes effect the moment the document is indexed. A fine-tuned model would need retraining.
It is restricted. Retrieval can respect who is allowed to see which document. Knowledge trained into a model is available to everyone who uses it.
It needs sources. A RAG answer can link each claim to the passage it came from, which is what lets a person check it.

sections.heading: When fine-tuning earns its cost
sections.text: Fine-tuning is worth considering when the task is narrow and repeated at high volume: classifying tickets into your own categories, writing in a strict house format, or extracting fields from a document type the base model handles poorly. It can also allow a smaller, cheaper model to do a job that otherwise needs a larger one. It requires hundreds to thousands of good examples and a way to measure the result.

sections.heading: What decides quality in a RAG system
sections.text: Most weak RAG systems fail at retrieval, not at the model. The parts that matter are how documents are split, whether search combines keywords with meaning, whether results are re-ranked, and whether the system admits when it found nothing relevant. Score retrieval and answer quality separately, so you know which one to fix.

sections.heading: A sensible order of work
sections.text: Start with good prompting and RAG over a small, clean set of documents. Build an eval set of real questions. Improve retrieval until the right passage is found reliably. Only then ask whether a remaining gap in tone, format or cost justifies fine-tuning.

faqs.question: Is RAG cheaper than fine-tuning?
faqs.answer: Usually at the start, because there is no training run and documents can be updated without retraining. At very high volume a fine-tuned smaller model can be cheaper per request, so the answer depends on scale.

faqs.question: Can we use both?
faqs.answer: Yes. A common pattern is a model fine-tuned for format or tone that still retrieves current facts through RAG.

faqs.question: Does RAG stop the model inventing answers?
faqs.answer: It reduces the risk but does not remove it. Add a grounding check that confirms each claim is supported by a retrieved passage, and send unsupported answers to a person.
